opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I like to think about it, and this is basically what we've been calling the LLM-Modulo framework, is that large language models are wonderful approximate retrieval engines. They're extraordinarily good at generating candidates: ideas, plan sketches, pieces of code, guesses about domain models. What they don't do, at least not in any guaranteed way, is verify. They don't reason in the sense of giving you correctness guarantees, and they certainly can't reliably critique their own output. We've done experiments on planning and constraint-satisfaction problems where you ask the model to self-critique, and performance often gets *worse*, because it can't tell when it was right and talks itself out of correct answers.

So rather than asking "can LLMs plan" or "can LLMs reason" in isolation, which I think is the wrong question, the more productive framing is: what role should they play in a larger system? In a compound system I'd put the LLM in a generate-test loop. It proposes, and a bank of external critics checks. Some critics are hard and sound: a plan validator, a model checker, a compiler, a simulator. Some are softer: style or preference critics, which might themselves be LLMs. The critiques get fed back, the LLM revises, and you iterate until the verifiers sign off. The guarantees come from the verifiers, not the generator.

The LLM can also help in other places. It can act as a knowledge source to help human experts build the domain models the verifiers need, which has historically been the bottleneck for classical planning. It can translate between the formal syntax of a solver and the natural language a user speaks. And it can reformat critiques so they're useful for another round.

What I push back on is the anthropomorphization: the assumption that because something sounds fluent, it must have reasoned its way to the answer. Even with the newer reasoning-style models that generate lots of intermediate tokens, I'd say those tokens shouldn't be read as faithful traces of thought. They're a way of getting better candidates, and you still want something sound downstream when correctness matters.

So my short answer: LLMs are a fantastic new component, maybe the most broadly useful one we've had in AI, but they're a component. The engineering, and the guarantees, come from how you compose them with things that actually check the work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts standalone planning or reasoning with using the LLM as a candidate generator in a larger system, where external verifiers provide the guarantees. This communicates a less demanding role within the compound system.

r002.rationale: The response describes iterative critique and revision but does not mention O1 Preview or say that critique-guided calls significantly improve its accuracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, you know, my basic position has been pretty consistent on this. I think large language models are fantastic idea generators. They are these amazing n-gram models on steroids, trained on essentially everything humanity has written, and so they can produce plausible candidates for almost anything you ask them about—plans, code, proofs, hypotheses. What they cannot do, by themselves, is guarantee that any of those candidates are correct. They don't reason in the sense we usually mean, they don't verify, they don't actually know what they don't know.

And so the way I've framed this, and we wrote about it in the LLM-Modulo paper, is that the right role for the LLM in a compound system is as a generator inside a generate-test loop. You have the LLM producing candidates, and then you have external critics—model-based verifiers, simulators, formal planners like VAL, even human critics—that check those candidates against hard constraints, and feed back the critique so the LLM can try again. That's the "modulo" part. The soundness guarantees come from the verifiers, not from the model. The LLM contributes the breadth, the world knowledge, the ability to translate between natural language and whatever formal representation your verifier needs.

What I push back on is this tendency to want the LLM to be the whole system—to do its own verification by, you know, "self-critique" or "chain of thought" and then claiming that's reasoning. Our own experiments showed that when you have the LLM critique itself, performance often gets worse, because the model is just as unreliable at verifying as at generating. Verification is in many cases a harder problem than generation, and you don't get it for free from the same autoregressive machinery.

So in a compound AI system, I'd say the LLM is the component that should be allowed to be wrong, and the architecture around it is what makes the overall system trustworthy. If you design it that way, you actually get something quite powerful—you combine the semantic flexibility of these models with the rigor of symbolic verifiers. If you don't, you end up with a system that's confidently wrong in exactly the places where it matters most.

r001.rationale: It assigns the model the narrower job of generating candidates and says external critics provide correctness guarantees, so the model need not make the whole system trustworthy on its own.

r002.rationale: It describes an external-critic generate-test loop, but does not mention O1 Preview or say critique-guided repeated calls significantly improve its accuracy.

astra-6.text:
I think language models have a very important role, but we should distinguish proposing a solution from establishing that the solution actually works. A language model can generate plausible ideas, possible plans, or candidate explanations. That is enormously useful. But plausibility is not a guarantee of correctness.

In a compound system, you can pair that generative ability with tools that check the candidates. Suppose you’re planning: the language model proposes a sequence of actions, and a verifier checks whether those actions satisfy the constraints and achieve the goal. If they don’t, the system can feed that information back and ask for another candidate. The assurance comes from the checking process, within the limits of what the checker can establish.

And there’s another useful role here: helping people articulate what they want. Often the problem specification itself is incomplete. A language model can support that conversation, although the human still needs to confirm that the resulting specification captures their intent.

So I see language models as powerful components for generating and communicating, embedded in an architecture that also provides verification and oversight. The interesting question is how those components work together, and which component is responsible for each claim of correctness.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models as generative components paired with verification and oversight, but never says their role in a compound system is less demanding than their role as a standalone system.

r002.rationale: It describes feeding verifier results back to request another candidate, but does not mention critique-guided repeated calls to O1 Preview or say that this significantly improves accuracy on some problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language models have a very useful role, but we should be careful about what responsibility we give them. They can propose possible solutions, translate a loosely stated request into something more structured, and bring in relevant knowledge. That makes them valuable components of a compound system. It doesn’t mean they can reliably certify that their own proposals are correct.

For planning, for example, I like the idea of an LLM-modulo framework: the language model generates a candidate plan, and external critics check it against the constraints of the problem. Does an action have its prerequisites satisfied? Does the plan actually achieve the goal? If a critic finds a problem, that feedback can guide another proposal. Some critics might be formal verifiers; others might involve a simulator or a human.

The important distinction is between generating a plausible candidate and establishing that it works. A language model can make the search much more flexible, especially when the initial problem is expressed in natural language. But whatever guarantees the overall system has must come from the checks we can actually justify. Putting several language models together doesn’t, by itself, give you that assurance.

r001.rationale: The response describes LLMs as useful components whose proposals need external checks, but it does not state that their role in a compound system is less demanding than their role as a standalone system.

r002.rationale: The response describes critics guiding another proposal, but it does not mention O1 Preview or claim that repeated critique-guided calls can significantly improve accuracy on some problems.
